extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (and patent practitioners reviewing subject-matter eligibility)
extracted.subtask_description: Apply the 2019 Patent Eligibility Guidance (PEG) two-step framework to determine whether a claimed invention recites statutory subject matter and whether it is directed to a judicial exception (and if so whether additional elements integrate the exception or supply an inventive concept).

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 1 — Statutory category
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate Step 1: Does this claim fall within a statutory category? (e.g., process, machine, manufacture, composition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim recites a series of steps it is to a process (Example language: 'Step 1 = Yes. The claim recites a series of steps, and thus, the claim is to a process.'). Determine whether the claim falls into one of the statutory categories before proceeding to Step 2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A Prong One — Identify abstract idea and mapping
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) Identify the specific limitation(s) in the claim that you believe recites an abstract idea, and (b) determine whether the identified limitation(s) falls within at least one of the groupings of abstract ideas enumerated in the 2019 PEG.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner should pinpoint claim limitations that potentially recite an abstract idea and then map those limitations to the enumerated groupings (mathematical concepts; mental processes; certain methods of organizing human activity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Enumerated groupings of abstract ideas (2019 PEG)
rubrics_metrics.description: Groupings include: Mathematical concepts; Mental processes; Certain methods of organizing human activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples/clarifications in the guidance: Mathematical concepts — mathematical relationships, formulas or equations, mathematical calculations. Mental processes — concepts performed in the human mind (including an observation, evaluation, judgment, opinion). Certain methods of organizing human activity — fundamental economic principles or practices (including hedging, insurance, mitigating risk), commercial or legal interactions (including agreements, advertising, marketing or sales activities), managing personal behavior or relationships (including social activities, teaching, following rules). Use these categories to determine whether an identified limitation is a judicial exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A Prong Two — Integration into a practical application
rubrics_metrics.description: Are there additional element(s) or a combination of elements in the claim that apply, rely on, or use the judicial exception in a manner that imposes a meaningful limit on the judicial exception, such that it is more than a drafting effort designed to monopolize the exception?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether additional claim elements impose meaningful limits or result in a specific improvement in technology or technical field. If so, the claim as a whole may integrate the abstract idea into a practical application (Example: the claim's specific manner of collecting additional NetFlow data when an abnormal condition is detected avoids excess network traffic and provides improved network monitoring).

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2B — Inventive concept (significantly more)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate Step 2B: Does the claim provide an inventive concept, i.e., does the claim recite additional element(s) or a combination of elements that amount to significantly more than the judicial exception in the claim?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If additional elements are merely nominal or routine computer implementation, they do not amount to significantly more. Example guidance: 'mere instructions to apply an exception using a generic computer component cannot ... provide an inventive concept.' If Step 2B = No, the claim does not provide an inventive concept and is ineligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic computer component limitation is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: A processor (or other generic computer component) recited at a high level of generality performing a generic computer function is no more than mere instructions to apply the exception using a generic computer component.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an additional element is simply a generic processor performing generic data processing tasks (e.g., determining amounts, ranking), it does not impose meaningful limits on practicing the abstract idea and therefore does not integrate the abstract idea into a practical application nor supply an inventive concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental process determination under broadest reasonable interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim limitation that, under its broadest reasonable interpretation, covers performance of the limitation in the human mind (or could practically be performed in the human mind) is a mental process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The mere nominal recitation of generic computer components (e.g., 'by the network appliance') does not necessarily remove the limitation from the mental processes grouping if the rest of the claim could be performed mentally. Example: 'comparing ... to a predefined threshold' may cover a user comparing values mentally and thus is a mental process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical concept requires explicit recitation
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim includes limitations that may be based upon mathematical relationships, formulas, or calculations, but those mathematical relationships/formulas/calculations are not explicitly recited in the claim, then the claim does not recite a mathematical concept for purposes of Step 2A Prong One.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat implicit or underlying math as a recited mathematical concept unless the claim explicitly recites mathematical formulas/relationships/calculations. (Example: digital simulation claim included math-based activity but did not explicitly recite a mathematical concept and thus was not treated as such.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate claim elements both individually and as a whole
rubrics_metrics.description: Elements that individually are mere pre- or post-solution activity may, in combination, yield a specific improvement and integrate the judicial exception into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the combination of elements recites a specific manner of achieving a technological improvement (e.g., targeted data collection to avoid excess network traffic and enable analysis). If the claim as a whole is directed to a particular improvement in computer-related technology or other field, it may be eligible despite component limitations being abstract when considered alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drafting a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 101 (examination/practice guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: When rejecting a claim as lacking subject matter eligibility under 35 U.S.C. 101, the rejection should: identify the abstract idea recited in the claim and include a reference to the appropriate enumerated grouping of abstract ideas; identify the additional elements and explain why they do not integrate the abstract idea into a practical application; and explain why the additional elements do not provide an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the 2019 PEG analysis structure in rejection wording. The training notes that new form paragraphs have been created for use with the 2019 PEG and that sample rejections are available on the microsite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outcome labeling guidance (Yes/No determinations)
rubrics_metrics.description: For each Step/Prong the examiner records an outcome (e.g., 'Step 1 = Yes', 'Step 2A = No', 'Step 2B = No') and an eligibility conclusion (claim is eligible or ineligible).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use explicit determinations for each stage. Examples: 'Step 2A = Yes. The claim is directed to the abstract idea.' or 'Step 2B = No, the claim does not provide an inventive concept. The claim is ineligible.' These labels clarify the analysis path and final conclusion.
